items.question: Why does starting more work make delivery slower rather than faster?

answer.text: At the same throughput, Little's law makes time in the system grow in proportion to work in progress, so every extra item started lengthens the wait for all of them.

items.question: Does limiting work in progress slow a team down?

answer.text: Not in the author's data: with limits, average cycle time fell from 31 to about 10 days while throughput stayed flat.

items.question: Is a per-person limit better than a team-wide limit?

answer.text: In the twelve-week comparison the per-person limit of 2 gave the shortest cycle time, 8.5 days against 10 for a team limit of 15;
the author cautions that it also makes swarming on a blocked item harder.

items.question: Where does the work go when a WIP limit says no?

answer.text: It waits upstream, where nobody measures it, so a limit hides a queue unless you also track what it turns away.

items.question: How should I choose a first WIP limit?

answer.text: Start from the work currently in progress and lower the limit step by step until items start waiting for people rather than people for items.
